data.title: JPMorgan Chase Raises Dividend 10%
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton 




  JPMorgan Chase raised its quarterly dividend to $1.65 from $1.50. 



  The dividend is payable on Oct. 31 to shareholders of record as of Oct. 6, the bank said Tuesday. 



  The new payout, equal to $6.60 a year, represents an annual payout of 1.9% based on Tuesday's closing price of $352.49.

data.title: 2 charts showing how oil is becoming the market's biggest wild card
data.description:
By Isabel Wang

Crude is increasingly 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime, a Nomura strategist warns

Oil is becoming a bigger problem for both stocks and long-term bonds.

Oil is increasingly calling the tune in global markets, as rising energy prices and worries about how much consumers are paying at the gas pump are making investors nervous and affecting their portfolios.

Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, higher oil prices have been bad news for both stocks and long-term Treasury bonds. When crude prices jump, stocks tend to fall. The same is true for long-duration government debt, as higher oil prices have been accompanied by falling bond prices and, in turn, higher yields.

That relationship has become much stronger over the past seven months, as shown in the charts below.

The Iran war appears to have marked a turning point in the relationship between oil and both stocks and Treasurys. Before the war, the relationship between U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude (CL00) (CL.1) (CLV26) and the S&P 500 SPX was basically neutral, with their rolling 63-day correlation at just 0.04 on Feb. 27. But by the end of March, it had fallen to minus 0.35, and by late April it had reached minus 0.48, according to Dow Jones Market Data. In other words, when oil prices rise, stocks have increasingly tended to fall.

A value closer to minus 1 means a perfect negative correlation between oil prices and stocks, while a number closer to 0 shows the relationship is very weak or even nonexistent.

The same pattern is showing up in long-term Treasurys. The rolling 63-day correlation between the U.S. oil benchmark and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF TLT fell to minus 0.28 by the end of April, from minus 0.15 on Feb. 27. It was at minus 0.55 on Tuesday morning, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

"Crude oil and energy is 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime," said Charlie McElligott, cross-asset macro strategist at Nomura Securities International.

Indeed, oil is increasingly behaving like a macro risk for equities, rather than simply another indicator of economic growth. Normally, higher oil prices can be bullish for stocks because they can signal stronger economic demand. That's partly why the correlation between WTI and the S&P 500 was mostly positive in 2025.

But now, the oil supply shock brought on by the Middle East conflict is propelling energy prices higher as transportation and production costs rise. At the same time, central banks are fighting to keep interest rates higher for longer. That matters to U.S. households because higher rates would directly increase the cost of borrowing money for mortgages, car loans and credit cards. They can also eat into American businesses' bottom lines, squeezing corporate margins and weighing on equity valuations.

"Treasury yields are now impacted less by safe-haven flows and more by inflation expectations, and the correlation between yields and oil prices is at its highest level for seven years," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

In other words, the oil shock is having a direct impact on U.S. financial conditions, Brooks told MarketWatch on Tuesday.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note BX:TMUBMUSD10Y was up 2 basis points Tuesday to trade at 5.040%, its highest intraday level since July 19, 2007. The 30-year Treasury rate BX:TMUBMUSD30Y was also up 2 basis points, at 5.369%, according to FactSet data.

"I've always found it somewhat odd that front-month oil correlates so highly to the 10-year Treasury [yield], but their increasingly synchronized moves reflect not only [that] inflation is at risk but real rates are backing up substantially," said Nate Shetty, chief investment officer at SEI Investments Company.

Real interest rates are nominal interest rates minus the inflation rate. When they rise substantially, it means money is genuinely becoming more expensive to borrow for U.S. consumers and businesses in terms of actual purchasing power.

"We are believers that Treasurys have lost their flight-to-quality positions," Shetty told MarketWatch in a phone interview on Tuesday. "In other words, the negative correlation we've seen in 20 years past between Treasurys and stocks has now flipped to the positive."

"Another way of saying this is that Treasurys are going to trade like risk assets, and in fact, they are," he said.

Of course, equities won't escape rising oil prices unscathed. "When the consequences of a geopolitical crisis roils oil markets and bruises the bond market, it is only a matter of time before equities get hit," Brooks of XTB added.

Opinion: Stocks have so far survived rising Treasury yields. But that may be about to change.

But aside from this week's tech selloff following calls from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other executives to slow artificial-intelligence development, U.S. stocks have been resilient. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA was off just 0.4% so far this quarter, while the S&P 500 has risen 1.2% and the Nasdaq Composite COMP was down 0.9%, according to FactSet data.

-Isabel Wang

data.title: Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards
data.description:
Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards

Merit Coffee Earns Two Gold Medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards

PR Newswire

SAN ANTONIO, Sept. 15, 2026

SAN ANTONIO, Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Merit Coffee Company, the Texas specialty coffee roaster known for its community-driven cafés and award-winning coffee program, has been awarded two gold medals at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards, an international competition recognizing excellence in coffee quality and roasting.

The two gold-medal-winning coffees include Lucem, Merit's "everyday blend," and a limited-edition Peru Gesha Natural that will debut as part of the company's upcoming holiday coffee rollout. Both coffees received top recognition following a rigorous double-blind evaluation by an international panel of certified coffee professionals.

Merit's Lucem Brand has become a signature part of Merit's coffee program and is one of the company's most widely available coffees. Utilizing coffees sourced from Honduras and Brazil, Lucem is sold across all 15 Merit cafés and is also available throughout Texas at retail partners including select H-E-B's, Whole Foods Market, Sprouts, Kroger, and Central Market. Lucem can also be ordered on Merit's online shop at MeritCoffee.com.

The second gold medal was awarded to a Peru Gesha Natural, offering an early glimpse at one of the coffees Merit will introduce during its holiday coffee rollout. The coffee will be released later this year, with additional details regarding its sourcing, character, and availability to be announced closer to its debut.

Both award winning coffees were roasted by Merit's Head Roaster & Q Grader, Carlos Riaño, who recently qualified for the United States Coffee Roasting Championship and will compete this December for a chance to advance to the global finals.

The Global Coffee Awards evaluates coffees solely on sensory quality, with judges assessing attributes including aroma, flavor, balance, sweetness, acidity, body, and overall cup performance. The competition also recognizes the collaborative work of producers and roasters in bringing exceptional coffees from farm to cup.

The two gold medals underscore Merit's continued commitment to sourcing exceptional coffees and thoughtfully roasting each coffee to highlight its unique qualities. The recognition also celebrates both a coffee that customers already know and love and an award-winning coffee that will soon make its way into their cups.

In addition to the two gold medals, five additional Merit coffees received bronze medals, bringing the company's total recognition at the 2026 Global Coffee Awards to seven medals. Camino de Oro, Patlanalan Community, Saddle Up, and Sugarcane Decaf were among the additional Merit coffees recognized, further highlighting the breadth and quality of the company's coffee program.

Additional details regarding the release of the Peru Gesha Natural and Merit's holiday coffee lineup will be announced through Merit Coffee's social media channels and website in the coming months.

About Merit Coffee

Founded in San Antonio in 2009, Merit Coffee is a Texas specialty coffee company dedicated to sourcing, roasting, and serving exceptional coffee. With cafés across San Antonio, Austin, Dallas, and Houston, Merit is committed to creating welcoming spaces where quality coffee, genuine hospitality, and community come together. Merit's coffees are available online, in cafés, and through retail partners across Texas.

Media Contact:
Charlie Paulette
charlie@meritcoffee.com

data.title: RUTGERS AND RWJBARNABAS HEALTH TO LAUNCH INNOVATION HUB, POWERED BY AMAZON WEB SERVICES
data.description:
RUTGERS AND RWJBARNABAS HEALTH TO LAUNCH INNOVATION HUB, POWERED BY AMAZON WEB SERVICES

RUTGERS AND RWJBARNABAS HEALTH TO LAUNCH INNOVATION HUB, POWERED BY AMAZON WEB SERVICES

PR Newswire

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J., Sept. 15, 2026

The collaboration establishes one of the nation's first technology innovation hubs that brings together a medical school, academic health system and cloud technology leader to advance patient care and medical education

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J., Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rutgers University and RWJBarnabas Health today announced the launch of the Rutgers/RWJBarnabas Health Innovation Hub, powered by Amazon Web Services.

This collaboration will provide opportunities for students studying medicine, engineering, computer science, business and other fields to work at the forefront of technology-driven discovery. By bringing together students, clinicians, researchers and technology experts, the hub will accelerate advancements in medical education, clinical innovation and patient care throughout New Jersey.

The hub combines Rutgers' academic and research abilities, RWJBarnabas Health's clinical expertise and patient reach as New Jersey's largest academic health system, and AWS cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) technology to tackle real-world health care challenges from the classroom to the hospital bedside. It also mirrors the state's efforts to ensure New Jersey maintains its legacy as a leader in innovation and invention.

"As we build the future Rutgers School of Medicine, we have an unprecedented opportunity to embed innovation into the foundation of how we educate and deliver care," said Amy Murtha, founding dean of the future Rutgers School of Medicine. "This collaboration with RWJBarnabas Health and AWS means our students won't just learn about the future of health care – they'll build solutions that can reach real patients in real communities across New Jersey."

"As New Jersey continues to lead in being a home for innovation, RWJBarnabas Health will lead by bringing to New Jersey a new model for integrating technologies that can change the way we deliver care, educate tomorrow's clinicians, and save lives," said Mark E. Manigan, president and chief executive officer of RWJBarnabas Health. "Along with our partners at Rutgers, this hub will allow us to take new technologies from ideation to implementation. We are ready to carry on our state's legacy of healthcare innovation leadership that Robert Wood Johnson began more than a century ago."

The long-term goal is a self-sustaining innovation model in which successful projects advance into Rutgers' academic enterprise and RWJBarnabas Health's clinical innovation efforts, attracting new collaborators, research support and industry partnerships that create opportunities for future student teams.

"What Rutgers and RWJBarnabas Health are building together is exactly the kind of bold, mission-driven collaboration we champion at AWS, bringing world-class cloud and AI technology to bear on challenges that truly matter," said Kim Majerus, vice president of global education and local government at Amazon Web Services. "They're creating an engine that will deliver real solutions for the people of New Jersey while preparing the next generation of health care professionals to lead with AI. When institutions come together like this – shoulder to shoulder, across disciplines – that's when we see the kind of transformation that changes lives."

Students throughout Rutgers, from undergraduates to doctoral students, will have the chance to participate in four- to 10-week rapid prototyping projects, which are short and intensive collaborations that design and test ideas.

The inaugural cohort is expected to include up to five interdisciplinary teams working on needs identified by Rutgers faculty and RWJBarnabas Health clinicians. Potential areas of focus may include technology tools that support clinical decision-making, medical and interprofessional education, student health and wellness, streamlined hospital operations and efforts to advance health equity.

Rutgers faculty and RWJBarnabas Health clinicians will mentor the teams and evaluate their projects as they develop and test their ideas. Students will have access to AWS technology, cloud computing credits, operational support, technical mentorship from AWS engineers and the broader AWS Cloud Innovation Centers network.

Housed in the Health and Life Science Exchange (HELIX) in New Brunswick, N.J., the hub will provide a dedicated home for interdisciplinary collaboration, where teams will develop solutions to pressing issues in health care education and delivery. The goal is to help move promising student ideas from prototypes toward real-world applications in research, medical education and patient care, including technologies that streamline hospital operations, strengthen care coordination and improve patient experience.

The HELIX also will be home to the New Brunswick campus of the future Rutgers School of Medicine, which will unite Robert Wood Johnson Medical School and New Jersey Medical School. Pending accreditation in 2027 from the Liaison Committee on Medical Education, the accrediting body for medical education programs, the first class of the unified school is expected to enroll in 2028 at what would become one of the nation's largest public medical schools based on enrollment.

Rutgers has seen the potential of interdisciplinary health care innovation through the Rutgers Health Hack, where students, faculty and industry partners including RWJBarnabas Health and AWS collaborate to address health care priorities during a 48-hour "hackathon."

One recent project involves developing an intelligent coaching system that uses students' academic progress to provide personalized AI-generated feedback and guidance alongside one-on-one coaching. The technology is being developed to support students at both Robert Wood Johnson Medical School and New Jersey Medical School as the schools integrate.

The Rutgers/RWJBarnabas Health Innovation Hub, powered by AWS, extends that model year-round, providing a structured pathway for promising projects to evolve from identified clinical needs to tested solutions.

Operations are expected to begin in the fall.

ABOUT RUTGERS, THE STATE UNIVERSITY OF NEW JERSEY
Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, is a leading national research university and the state of New Jersey's preeminent, comprehensive public institution of higher education. Established in 1766, the university is the eighth-oldest higher education institution in the United States. More than 71,000 students and 27,000 faculty and staff learn, work, and serve the public at Rutgers University-New Brunswick, Rutgers University-Newark, Rutgers University-Camden and Rutgers Health. 

ABOUT RWJBARNABAS HEALTH
RWJBarnabas Health is New Jersey's largest and most comprehensive academic health system, caring for more than five million people annually. Nationally renowned for quality and safety, the system includes 14 hospitals and 9,000 affiliated physicians integrated to provide care at more than 700 patient care locations.

RWJBarnabas Health partners with its communities to build and sustain a healthier New Jersey. It provides patient-centered care in a compassionate manner and is the state's largest safety-net provider and leader in addressing the social determinants of health. RWJBarnabas Health provides food to the hungry, housing for the homeless and economic opportunities to those most vulnerable. 

RWJBarnabas Health's commitment to enhancing access to care includes a transformative partnership with Rutgers University, including the Rutgers Cancer Institute — the state's only NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School.

RWJBarnabas Health is among New Jersey's largest private employers, with more than 45,000 employees, contributing more than $7 billion to the state economy every year. For more information, visit www.RWJBH.org.

ABOUT AMAZON WEB SERVICES
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is guided by customer obsession, pace of innovation, commitment to operational excellence, and long-term thinking. By democratizing technology for nearly two decades and making cloud computing and generative AI accessible to organizations of every size and industry, AWS has built one of the fastest-growing enterprise technology businesses in history. Millions of customers trust AWS to accelerate innovation, transform their businesses, and shape the future. With the most comprehensive AI capabilities and global infrastructure footprint, AWS empowers builders to turn big ideas into reality. Learn more at aws.amazon.com and follow @AWSNewsroom.

CONTACTS:

Carrie.cristello@rwjbh.org

data.title: Why a Federal Reserve rate hike could be a 'rare win' for your retirement money
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

There may be better savings yields, but beware rising credit-card rates

Nearly half of Americans aged 50 and older carry credit-card debt from month to month, including debt on active cards or cancelled cards, according to AARP.

Retirees may benefit from this week's expected interest-rate hike by earning more money on cash kept in CDs, high-yield savings accounts or money-market funds. Still, those gains may be offset by higher interest rates on credit cards and overall higher costs of living.

"Higher rates are a rare win for anyone living off savings instead of a paycheck," said Jeff Judge, a financial adviser and managing partner with Chesapeake Financial Planners. "The same rate hike that helps a CD also punishes anyone carrying a credit-card balance."

The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the wake of the recent surge in oil prices, a strong jobs report and persistent inflation. While some economists predict a series of rate hikes, any increase would be the first from the Fed since 2023, and the first under Kevin Warsh's tenure as chairman.

With potentially higher interest rates "there are real positives here. Retirees who've built up cash reserves finally get paid something for holding safe assets. CDs, money markets and high-yield savings accounts all move up with the Fed, and for someone living off a fixed income, that extra yield on a CD ladder is real, spendable money," Judge said.

Another benefit for older adults: Buying an annuity when rates are high can provide a larger regular payout, advisers said.

While higher expected interest rates have some benefits for older adults holding cash, there are some instances when they can hurt seniors, especially those with debt. Nearly half of Americans aged 50 and older carry over credit-card debt from month to month, including debt on active cards or cancelled cards, according to AARP.

"Credit-card debt gets more expensive fast, since most cards carry variable rates tied directly to the prime rate. And seniors carry credit-card debt more often than people assume, sometimes to cover a medical bill or a grandkid's tuition gap," Judge said. "If they're only making minimum payments, a rate increase can turn a manageable balance into a much bigger problem within a year."

The simplest way to think about higher interest rates is that they generally help seniors who are net savers and hurt those who are net borrowers, said Jon Lapp, a financial adviser and founder of Haven Financial Advisors.

"To benefit from higher rates, seniors should first make sure idle cash is actually earning a competitive return. Many traditional savings accounts continue to pay far less than online savings accounts, CDs or Treasurys. A CD or Treasury ladder can spread maturities over time, preserve regular access to money, and reduce the risk of locking everything up at one rate," Lapp said.

Keep near-term spending money liquid, match bond maturities to expected expenses and avoid making bets about where rates will go next, Lapp said.

Rising rates make HELOCs (home equity lines of credit) and adjustable-rate mortgages "unpredictable at exactly the point in life when predictability matters most," Judge said.

"Don't lock long-term CDs the moment rates rise, thinking you've caught the top. And don't ignore a credit-card balance because 'it's just the minimum.' The math on variable-rate debt moves against seniors faster than most people expect." Judge said.

Overall, "higher interest rates can be a mixed bag for seniors," said Kashif Ahmed, founder and president of American Private Wealth.

"Higher rates ... make borrowing more expensive, especially credit-card debt and variable-rate loans. And seniors shouldn't assume that all bonds are unaffected - when rates rise, existing bond prices generally fall," Ahmed said.

"The biggest thing to avoid is making a dramatic change to a retirement portfolio simply because rates have moved. The right strategy is still one that balances income, liquidity, inflation protection and long-term growth," Ahmed said.

For those on fixed incomes or rigid budgets, like many retirees, "inflation can be especially dangerous," said Randy Bruns, a financial adviser and founder of Model Wealth Inc. "Workers have some inherent inflation protection through their 'human capital,' as wages tend to adjust upward over time. Retirees living primarily off financial capital don't have that same natural hedge."

That is one reason Social Security is incredibly valuable to retirees, Bruns said.

"Every dollar of guaranteed income reduces the amount retirees must draw from their investment portfolios, improving the sustainability of their retirement plan. When that income is also inflation-protected, as Social Security is, its value is even greater. For many Americans, Social Security may be the most valuable component of their retirement cash flow," he said.

Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 could rise about $71 a month, analysts said after the August consumer-price index was released last week. A higher COLA reflects an increase to help beneficiaries keep pace with inflation.

Social Security, however, faces insolvency in 2032, at which time benefits will be automatically cut by 22% unless Congress acts to shore up the system.

"Retirees may be earning more on money markets, CDs and Treasury bills, but those higher rates are likely being offset by higher inflation. In many cases, their returns are simply moving in lockstep with their rising cost of living," Bruns said.

-Jessica Hall

data.title: Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard Explains Home Remodel Cost Factors in HelloNation
data.description:
Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard Explains Home Remodel Cost Factors in HelloNation

Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard Explains Home Remodel Cost Factors in HelloNation

PR Newswire

SOMERSET, Ky., Sept. 15, 2026

The Article Explains How Project Scope, Existing Conditions, Labor, Structural Work, and Material Choices Shape a Remodeling Budget

SOMERSET, Ky., Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What determines the cost of a home remodel? A HelloNation article answers that question, featuring insights from Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard of Secure Structure in Somerset, Kentucky.

The HelloNation article explains that home remodel cost depends on more than square footage or the number of rooms being renovated. Project scope, existing conditions, structural changes, materials, labor requirements, and finish selections can all influence the final remodeling budget.

According to the article, project scope is one of the largest factors affecting home remodeling costs. Cosmetic work may involve flooring, paint, cabinets, or fixtures, while larger renovations can require moving walls, replacing plumbing, upgrading electrical systems, or changing heating and cooling equipment.

The article notes that structural changes can add complexity because they may require specialized trades and additional planning. Removing a wall, for example, can involve determining whether it supports the structure above and whether new framing or a support beam is needed.

Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard is featured as a source of insight into how these project details affect costs. The article describes why evaluating the planned work before construction begins gives homeowners a clearer foundation for building a realistic remodeling budget.

Kitchen renovation projects often cost more because several building systems must be coordinated in one space. The article explains that cabinetry, countertops, appliances, plumbing, electrical wiring, lighting, flooring, and ventilation may all contribute to the overall home remodel cost.

Bathroom remodeling can involve similar challenges. Waterproofing, plumbing fixtures, tile, ventilation, electrical work, and cabinetry may be required, while moving a shower, toilet, or sink can increase costs when existing plumbing must be changed.

Material and finish selections also play an important role in home remodeling costs. The article notes that cabinets, countertops, flooring, tile, fixtures, and appliances come in broad price ranges, so similar layouts can produce significantly different budgets.

Labor requirements vary with the amount and complexity of the work. Projects involving electricians, plumbers, carpenters, tile installers, and other skilled trades can require additional labor hours, scheduling, and coordination.

The article also explains that existing conditions are sometimes difficult to identify before construction begins. Opening walls or floors may reveal water damage, outdated wiring, deteriorated plumbing, or structural problems. Older homes may also require updates to meet current building codes during renovation.

A detailed project scope helps homeowners understand which parts of the renovation drive the overall price. The article explains that defining what will be removed, repaired, changed, and installed creates a stronger basis for estimating costs before work starts.

Changes during construction can affect both the remodeling budget and project schedule. New features, different materials, or layout revisions may require additional labor, materials, permits, or adjustments to connected parts of the project.

The HelloNation article concludes that a remodeling budget should reflect the specific home and planned work, not just a general price per square foot. By considering project scope, existing conditions, labor, structural changes, and finishes together, homeowners can better understand why estimates vary. Construction Expert Jon-Brent Bernard provides the industry perspective featured throughout the article.

What Determines the Cost of a Home Remodel? Features insights from Jon-Brent Bernard, Construction Expert of Somerset, Kentucky, in HelloNation.

data.title: Top Senate Republican floats a diesel export ban as prices soar. It might not work.
data.description:
By Claudia Assis

With diesel prices hitting a record $6.27 a gallon, Washington is talking about a maneuver that could ultimately make matters worse

The U.S. is the world's largest exporter of diesel.

The Senate's top Republican said he's open to discussing an export ban on diesel as the price of the fuel reached new heights on Tuesday.

The average price of diesel in the U.S. hit an all-time high of $6.27 per gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA, up about 80 cents from a month ago. A year ago, the price was $3.69 a gallon.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday that he's open to exploring a diesel export ban as one way to take pressure off diesel prices.

With the midterm elections about seven weeks away and the war with Iran at an impasse, that could be a Band-Aid solution to curb prices in the near term. Market participants are quick to point out, however, that an export ban would make matters worse in the long run and would be ineffectual in a free-market economy.

A White House spokesperson declined to say whether the Trump administration is considering a ban, pointing instead to comments by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who on Monday said that an export ban on crude oil or fuels would be unlikely to ?help lower retail energy prices.

The White House official also referred to comments made Monday by Jarrod Agen, executive director of the administration's National Energy Dominance Council, who told CNBC the public would soon be hearing about "energy deals" to help bring down energy prices.

Diesel is the economy's workhorse fuel, powering heavy-duty vehicles and machinery. Higher diesel prices probably hit the economy "sooner than gasoline does," said Eric Smith, a professor at Tulane University and associate director of the Tulane Energy Institute.

The U.S. is the world's largest exporter of diesel, with Russia being No. 2.

U.S. distillate inventories, which include diesel, are 13% below their five-year average, according to the latest report from the Energy Information Administration. Gasoline inventories are 5% below their five-year average, the EIA said.

Russia has placed a ban on its own diesel exports through the end of September and is widely expected to extend that moratorium. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, in response to deadly Russian strikes in Ukraine, have crippled several Russian refineries, putting more pressure on global diesel prices and sending countries that would otherwise be able to import Russian diesel scrambling to find the fuel elsewhere. That has made diesel scarcer - and more expensive - globally.

See also: It's not just Hormuz. Another war is providing fresh price shocks to fuel and food.

While a U.S. ban on diesel exports might bring some relief to diesel prices in the short term, its longer-term consequences could potentially be "devastating," said Rebecca Babin, a senior energy trader and managing director at CIBC Private Wealth.

It would be very negative for U.S. refiners and would push global energy prices higher, hitting U.S. prices as well, because the country does not domestically produce all the fuels and crude products it needs, she said.

With an export ban in place, U.S. refiners would likely drop their diesel production significantly, but the U.S. would still need to import certain grades of gasoline and other fuels, Babin said. Those fuel products could become more expensive as refineries outside the U.S. pivot to meet the excess global demand for diesel.

"It's a global market," she said. "[U.S. refiners] would just cut their runs to meet domestic demand," possibly providing some short-term relief.

Ultimately, however, a ban would stress U.S. producers and refiners and ultimately keep the global market "really tight and high," she said.

Victor Reklaitis contributed.
